O1:
I'm opening a residency for artists, writers and designers in Taiwan in 2033, and before I ask for anything, here is where it stands.

Its running costs, $50,000 every January from 2033 to 2042, are already paid for. Each payment comes from a US Treasury held for me that matures just before its January, bought in January 2027 and completed in January 2028. I'm not asking anyone for this money.

I will give $115,000 to build the residency's facility, paid in December 2032, before the building's first draw in 2033. $95,000 of it has been held for me in Treasuries since January 2028, and the rest since my shares moved into Treasuries in January 2031. It is fixed in US dollars and won't rise if the building costs more.

I'm asking for two things. First, capital for the facility, pledged on one condition: that the total set in the residency's budget is reached by a single close date, no later than December 2032, so every conditional pledge releases together. Mine comes first and carries no condition. Second, yearly programme money from 2033, one year at a time, the way Taiwan's funders give.

Both go to the residency itself, its own body in Taiwan, which owns the site and runs the building. I won't ask you to match my figure, and neither the ten payments nor the rest of my money is part of this offer.

The custodian holding the Treasuries can send you a statement on request.

Laura

O3:
Our advisor handled administration only; we made the decisions and wrote our own IPS.

Our first Big Idea was that Laura's first $300,000 could buy Treasuries for all ten payments on its own. Our notes called it "very tight", and it was. Our orders filled on 7 and 8 October, within two trading days of the year's cheapest close, and that was luck, not skill – the market opened at 00:30 Sydney time on the 7th, and Eric was asleep before it did. Priced at every close of 2026, the ten cost less than $300,000 only from September into early November, and on 16 October the room left was about $1,900. So the 2028 deposit got a first job: if the ten ever cost more than $300,000, it finishes them before it does anything else.

The case pulls Laura two ways: she is "willing to take thoughtful risks", and her payments must be met "with a high degree of certainty". On 27 September our first plan followed the first phrase – about three-quarters shares. We dropped it before any trade, and the reason was Laura's work, not the market. Our notes that day already called her income "lumpy": advances, fees and licences come later and smaller in the same recessions that knock shares down, so shares would have been falling just when her income was. Our first model only priced the change. The first plan missed at least one payment in about 1 in 31 runs; the Treasury plan misses none once the 2028 deposit's first dollars arrive. Most people would call 30 in 31 "high" certainty – we didn't keep it, because of how Laura is paid. The model also showed the danger wasn't a crash: the first plan needed share prices in the right place on one date, 1 January 2033, when all ten payments had to be bought with whatever the shares had become.

The shares had their own argument. On 30 September, before anyone objected, we wrote down the bar an alternative had to clear to replace the one world fund, VT, and only then ran the numbers. We tested four, from American shares alone to VT with some gold and property trusts beside it. None cleared the bar; gold and property came closest, mostly by cutting off the good outcomes. Then on 5 October Darren called one world fund a "copout" and wanted us to pick stocks and ETFs like a normal team; a Taiwan fund and gold came up too. We decided, in the end, to keep the one world fund. Before, VT had been a sensible default, cheap and spread wide; after, we could say why it suits Laura in particular. It's the one holding allowed to be wrong, and it can only be wrong along with the whole market – and most single US stocks have done worse than Treasury bills over their lives (Bessembinder, 2018). It needs no opinions, so it never becomes a third reason to change the plan. And a Taiwan fund would only add more Taiwan to a plan whose building is already there.

Two recommendations changed and one held: the payments left shares for Treasuries because of how Laura is paid, the 2028 deposit got its first job because the room under $300,000 nearly ran out, and the world fund stayed, now for reasons that are about Laura.

C1: We know Treasury bonds (including this one – maturing 2037) won't create wealth, but they will remove uncertainty, through duration-matching. In other words, we take Laura's requested 'high degree of certainty' to mean a near-ironclad guarantee, and we provide exactly that. Every year the bonds sit untouched is a good year – one less year of Laura's money being exposed to anything the restless markets might decide to do. Notably – Laura's payments are fixed in nominal dollars, so a nominal Treasury matches the liability perfectly, meaning we don't need TIPS, which would hedge against a nonexistent inflation risk.
C2: Some years, WInS lists no Treasuries maturing – so we purchased iShares iBonds (like IBTM for 2032) instead. Defined-maturity, investment-grade, liquid, cheap and transparent about yields, these behave a lot like bonds when held to their end – so we'll simply ignore price noise in the interim. Together, our T-Bonds and iBonds ensure each of Laura's payments rests on a dedicated instrument (not merely a forecast). The catch is, their terminal payout is a net asset value, as opposed to a promise of par – but in return we gain a level of liquidity which no odd-lot bond offers.
C3: VT is where we allow ourselves to be wrong – because it's the only investment not standing between Laura and a payment deadline. This ETF owns thousands of companies, diversified across countries and sectors, which means we can avoid paying the price for the vain illusion that we can pick winners, instead buying the entire market's growth premium at an expense ratio of just 0.06%, for a forecast return of about 7.5% a year (as per JPMorgan). The T-Bonds and iBonds already cover the operating commitments, so VT answers a different question – how generous can the facility contribution be?
X1: Pension funds cover fixed payments either by matching their bonds' average life to the payments and rebalancing as rates move, or by buying one bond per payment and holding it. We do the second, which needs no forecast or trading. In January 2027, her first $300,000 buys a ladder of Treasury bonds and Treasury funds with fixed end dates, each maturing just before a January payment. A Treasury held to maturity pays exactly what it promised, whatever markets do, so no payment depends on shares.
X2:
In 2031, Laura gives co-sponsors a range. The bottom is the floor, rounded down: money she already owns. The top adds half her shares, which move into Treasuries before she names it, because a number said aloud can't quietly be halved after a bad year. The other half stays hers and liquid, as a cushion if the building costs more in Taiwan dollars.

The ladder's one weakness is that it counts on reinvesting its bonds' interest; if rates fall and stay low, it can fall short. Before Laura names her range, we price that shortfall at the day's rates, add a margin, and move that much from her kept shares into Treasuries. Her spare money shrinks before her promise does, and if it can't cover the gap, the whole range comes down.
